seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I received a mysterious £5 cheque of yours which I cashed with great difficulty, Miss Beach being away. The only cheque I can cash easily is an uncrossed cheque payable to me drawn by a London bank on its Paris branch or correspondent in French francs. Such a cheque can be bought by anyone sending me money at the bank where the person has an account in London, the amount (in £.s.d.) being charged against the person’s account.

What money is this £5? Is it
Dial money? Or your own?
As regards the £10: send it. I shall pay it back out of the first American remittance. Now let me comment a few of your phrases:
Colleagues: Yes. That is what I think. What other kind of conduct, then, is that of yourself and also of Mr Rodker towards me?
Despised £5 of Pinker : Nay more, of despised Pinker. The buying value of £5 = prewar £1.4 = 28/-. We are four in family: 28 ÷ 4 = 7/-. I cannot become enthusiastic about 7/-.

Fritz’s punch : This concoction is not punch. On the other hand he cooks solid food well enough. He invited me to dinner where I delayed the table at each course by meditative eating and paralysed conversation by glances of gloomy preoccupation and excited gentle mirth by addressing the gentlemen as Monsieur and the ladies as Madame contrary to the usages of polite society.
Sassenach blood: I have not perceived much of that condiment in you.

Stimulants: No. Relaxatives. By the way l’ami Fritz believes that I am a wholehearted consumer of strong spirits (as a matter of fact I dislike them) and insists with rollicking Dutch humour in offering me goblets of some horrible stuff called l’eau de vie du Midi or l’eau de mort de Minuit I don’t know which. I see that your airiest word sways the heads of the three colonies to which you presented me here. Breaking a silence of several hours I ventured to express an appreciation of a certain very uncoloured, very dry wine of the Rhine – a remark which was howled down.

Ulysses : Thanks for your interest in this book. I am cursedly weary of it but must finish it. You are wrong in thinking that you made a bad impression on me either here or in Sermione . I perceived that you were rushed off your feet and that I myself was constantly casting myself at your feet. My fits of abstraction are not due to illtemper but to real preoccupation of a threefold nature: poetic, personal, and family.

Imbecile: Applying this to myself I meant in following the will o’ the wisp which I follow when I have or had a number of other possibilities. I dislike writing and dislike the people I write for – I mean the public. “Joy of creation”! However even in the wider sense I have no objection to being so described.

Warsaw : I saw this name in a paper. It is known to me as the present residence of sir Horace Rumbold . Do not be alarmed. He is emphatically the right man in the wrong place. The enclosed verses may be posted without billstamp.

postscript.p: P.S. I forgot to say thanks for the cheque (£5). I paid police fees, gas bill, baker and milk and will hobble onward a little farther with Madam Circe’s herd.

div.note: Sylvia Beach (1887-1962), American owner of the Paris bookstore Shakespeare and Company (then at 8 rue Dupuytren, later at 12 rue de l’Odéon) and publisher of the first edition of Ulysses in Paris in February 1922. When JJ had difficulty cashing a check in Paris, he sometimes gave it to Beach, who would deposit it in her account and pay JJ the amount (LIII 12). JJ had met her at a literary gathering at the home of French poet and critic André Spire (1868–1966) in Neuilly on 11 July 1920. He went to see her at her bookstore the next day (Ellmann, JJ 488-89). Their long friendship and collaboration were among the most important developments of literary modernism.

An uncrossed or open check was one for which the payee or bearer could obtain payment from any bank. A crossed check, so indicated by lines drawn across its face, could be paid only through a particular account. An uncrossed check was therefore easier to cash. (For an example in literature, see H.G. Wells, Ann Veronica: A Modern Love Story [New York: Harper & Brothers, 1909], 162.)

Pound was casting about – from various sources including his own bank account – for ways to assist JJ financially in his first months in Paris. Pound was a paid agent and foreign correspondent for the New York magazine The Dial at this time and had recruited contributions from JJ and many other European authors. JJ’s sole contribution was his poem, “A Memory of the Players in a Mirror at Midnight,” printed in vol. 69, no. 1 (July 1920): 26, and later included in his volume, Pomes Penyeach (1927).

JJ was hoping that Pound could send him £10 as a loan, to be secured by his expectation of a royalty payment from his American publisher B.W. Huebsch or a sum sent by the New York lawyer and art patron John Quinn, who was making installment payments on a purchase of JJ’s Ulysses manuscript. (For fuller accounts, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes; 24 July 1920, notes.) Pound replied to JJ’s request in his letter of 10 August 1920: “First American remittance is insufficient security … as the only person I can borrow the £10/ from, is an orphan. Also, if you want to borrow money, there is no reason why yr. solicitors shdnt now advance you £10/ on yr. Sept. installment [of interest payments from a trust settled on JJ by Harriet Shaw Weaver]. Thus saving me the bloody fuss of gathering same from not particularly willing furze bushes” (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 537). Nevertheless, Pound enclosed a gift of money, possibly his own, in his 10 August letter (see ibid.; JJ to Pound, 13 August 1920, notes).

Here, JJ is evidently citing and commenting on phrases from a letter by Pound that has not come to light. In his 10 August 1920 letter, Pound referred to JJ’s present letter as “yr. museum piece,” possibly because the cited and glossed phrases reminded him of museum exhibits with explanatory placards or labels (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 537).

JJ was grateful for moral and financial assistance at this time from Pound and John Rodker (1894-1955), English writer, poet, and publisher (for a fuller account of Rodker, see JJ to Pound, letter fragment, late July 1920, notes).

JJ had grown impatient waiting for royalties and sums from various sources, and urging his London literary agent J.B. Pinker (prob. 1862 or 1863-1922) to collect and send these on to him (LI 143) (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes).

Fritz-René Vanderpyl (1876-1965), Belgian (often described as Dutch) novelist, poet, gastronome, and art critic for Le Petit Parisien. JJ enjoyed the time he spent in Paris with this ebullient, talkative writer. Later in this letter, JJ refers to Vanderpyl’s “Dutch humour,” as he apparently spoke and read Dutch (see LIII 472). (For a fuller account of Vanderpyl, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes).

JJ was defensively aware of his habit in Paris of “addressing people I have just met for the first time as ‘Monsieur’” and the reputation he was earning for being “a tout petit bourgeois” (LI 166). The reference to “Monsieur” in this letter caused Pound to tease JJ by saluting him as “Monsieur” in his reply dated 10 August 1920 (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 537). JJ returned the volley by writing Pound a long, extra-polite letter, entirely in mock-formal French (see JJ to Pound, 13 August 1920, notes).

“Sassenach” is a somewhat derogatory term meaning the English or an English person when used by an Irish or Scottish person. In Ulysses, when Buck Mulligan is pretending to join forces with Stephen Dedalus against the Englishman Haines, who is temporarily staying with them, he says, before breakfast: “The Sassenach wants his morning rashers” (U 1.232). In the “Cyclops” episode, the violently nationalistic citizen charges that, during the Irish famine of the 1840s, “the Sassenach tried to starve the nation [Ireland] at home while the land was full of crops that the British hyenas bought and sold in Rio de Janeiro” (U 12.1369-71).
L’eau de vie du Midi can refer to various distilled liquors, often brandies, that have a high alcoholic content and are produced in southern France.

JJ is probably referring here to a Swiss white wine, Fendant de Sion, that became his favorite in Zurich and that he drank often with Frank Budgen, Ottocaro Weiss, and other friends at the Pfauen Café and other haunts. JJ and his companions referred to this light, dry vintage as “the Archduchess,” having decided that its pale gold was the color of a royal Austrian lady’s urine. JJ drank it on at least one occasion with Fritz Vanderpyl and the French writer Edmond Jaloux (1878-1949) at a restaurant in the rue St. Honoré (Ellmann, JJ 492). JJ here calls it a “very dry wine of the Rhine,” but the town of Sion, in the canton of Valais, is along the Rhône River.

JJ and Pound met for the first time in Sirmione, Italy, in June 1920. Afterwards, Pound wrote John Quinn that he found JJ “pleasing; after the first shell of cantankerous Irishman, I got the impression that the real man is the author of Chamber Music. The sensitive: the rest is the genius; the registration of realities on the … delicate temperament of the early poems” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 189). For a more complete account of the Sirmione summit, see JJ telegram to Pound, 26 May 1920, notes.

After becoming embroiled in a minor legal dispute in Zurich in 1918, JJ sought help from, among others, Sir Horace Rumbold (1869-1941), the British Minister in Berne, but without success. He came to believe that Rumbold and certain British consular officials were instigating boycotts of performances by the English Players – the acting troupe that JJ cofounded and managed in Zurich – and he wrote a statement, dated 28 April 1919, setting forth the history of perceived outrages (LII 438-40). JJ never tired of exacting literary revenges on Rumbold, whom he cast in Ulysses as a “Master Barber” whose semi-literate letter offering his services as a hangman to the sheriff of Dublin is read out, to the contempt and ridicule of the pub drinkers, in the “Cyclops” episode (U 12.412-442). (For a fuller account of the Zurich litigation and the Rumbold affair, see JJ to Pound, 1 April 1919, notes.)

note.p: JJ’s enclosure of “verses” has not come to light, but they were almost certainly the anti-Rumbold lines, or a version of them, that he sent to Claud W. Sykes on 27 August 1920, alluding to Rumbold’s appointment as British ambassador to Poland:

l.hi: The Right Man in the Wrong Place

note.p: JJ sent a slightly different version of these verses, again attacking Rumbold, to his brother Stanislaus, also on 27 August (LIII 16).

div.note: Adhesive bill stamps had to be placed on certain negotiable instruments, such as promissory notes or money orders, passing between debtors and creditors residing in different countries, and often required special payment of ad valorem duty (see William Thomson, Dictionary of Banking: A Concise Encyclopædia of Banking Law and Practice, 5th ed. [London: Sir Isaac Pitman & Sons, 1924], 96).

The Paris prefecture of police issued permis de séjour (permits of sojourn) to foreigners for temporary visits lasting longer than a certain number of days (see JJ to Pound, letter fragment, late July 1920, notes).

At this time, JJ was working on “Circe,” the fifteenth and longest episode of Ulysses. Its dominant theme is the transformation of humans into beasts, and it draws a loose, phantasmagoric parallel between the Dublin brothel district of 1904 and the island of the witch Circe in Homer’s The Odyssey. Circe’s magic turns Odysseus’s crew into penned pigs (which JJ here calls “Madam Circe’s herd”), just as Bella Cohen’s bawdyhouse changes Dubliners into bestial buyers and sellers of pleasure. For a fuller account of “Circe,” see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1920, notes.
